headline: PAGASA Forecasts Up to Seven More Tropical Cyclones Before Year-End
seoTitle: PAGASA Forecasts Up to Seven More Cyclones in 2026 | FMB News
seoDescription: PAGASA expects five to seven tropical cyclones to form within or enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility from September through December 2026.
deck: The state weather bureau expects five to seven tropical cyclones from September through December while El Niño raises the risk of below-normal rainfall in parts of the country.
author: FMB News Desk

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: PAGASA expects five to seven more tropical cyclones to form within or enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility before the end of 2026, according to its updated seasonal outlook released Wednesday.

The monthly breakdown calls for two or three cyclones in September and one or two in each of October, November and December. These are seasonal ranges, not forecasts of specific tracks, intensity or landfall locations.

sections.heading: Context
paragraphs: The cyclone outlook comes as El Niño conditions are present in the tropical Pacific. PAGASA has warned that the warming pattern increases the likelihood of below-normal rainfall and dry spells, although individual tropical cyclones can still produce intense rain, flooding, rough seas and storm surge.

The next unused names on PAGASA's 2026 list begin with Pilandok, Queenie, Rosal, Samuel and Tomas. A name is assigned only when a system develops into or enters the agency's area as a tropical cyclone.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: The simultaneous risk of cyclones and seasonal drying requires local governments, farms, water utilities and households to plan for both short bursts of hazardous rain and longer periods of reduced water supply. The forecast ranges are planning guidance and will change as actual weather systems develop.

sections.heading: What to watch next
paragraphs: Watch PAGASA's monthly climate assessments and shorter-range tropical cyclone advisories for changes in expected activity. Track-specific warnings, rainfall forecasts and local evacuation notices should guide immediate safety decisions rather than the seasonal totals alone.
